subtitle: Some case, program and oversight decisions involve people with psychiatric disabilities. Learn to bring disability rights, a recovery orientation and Minnesota crisis resources into those decisions.
audience: For Disability Services Division staff, case managers and care coordinators, lead agencies, 245D provider oversight staff, and program, policy and supervisory staff who serve or make decisions affecting people with mental illness, including people who also have intellectual or developmental disabilities.

lessons.title: Psychiatric disability is disability
objectives: Explain why a mental health condition can be a disability under the ADA and Section 504.
Describe the Olmstead decision and the conditions the Supreme Court set for community-based services.
Distinguish the binding court decision from shifting federal enforcement guidance.
Identify when to route a rights question to the ADA coordinator or legal counsel.
lessons.teaching:
Mental health care and disability services may both matter to the same person. The Americans with Disabilities Act, or ADA, and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act protect people with qualifying mental impairments as well as physical impairments. A mental impairment can qualify when it substantially limits a major life activity, such as sleeping, thinking or working. Symptoms may vary over time or be difficult for others to see. Under the ADA, an episodic impairment is assessed by its limits when active. A period of fewer symptoms does not by itself remove protection. The ADA also covers a record of disability and being regarded as disabled, under different conditions. Eligibility for a specific service is a separate question.

Olmstead shows how closely mental health and disability services can be tied. Two Georgia women with mental illness and intellectual disabilities remained in a state hospital after their treatment professionals found community care appropriate. The Supreme Court held that unjustified segregation is discrimination under Title II of the ADA. Its ruling set conditions for community-based treatment: state treatment professionals find it appropriate, the person does not oppose it, and the state can reasonably accommodate it. That last condition takes account of the state’s resources and the needs of others it serves.

Minnesota’s Olmstead Plan sets goals for state agencies in housing, employment, person-centered planning, transportation and other areas. Federal views about enforcement can change. On June 18, 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice Office of Legal Counsel issued a narrower reading of Olmstead than earlier federal guidance. Minnesota’s Olmstead office described this as a departure from the long-standing view and affirmed the state’s commitment to its work. An executive-branch opinion does not overturn a Supreme Court decision. The next state plan remains a draft on Minnesota’s website. Ask counsel which current requirements apply to a decision; an older guidance page or draft plan cannot settle that question.

Notice when a decision may affect rights as well as care. A meeting time, deadline or service rule may prevent a person from taking part because of their disability. Ask about the barrier and make changes within your role, without assuming that you know what the person needs. Route formal questions about ADA duties, reasonable modifications and legal risk to the ADA coordinator or counsel. Provide the facts and the unresolved question so that the person or area responsible can assess it.
lessons.keyPoint: Psychiatric disability can raise disability-rights and service-access questions. Explore barriers with the person, make changes within your role and route formal determinations to the person or area responsible.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Marisol, a lead agency case manager, supports Terrence, who receives waiver services and has a psychiatric disability. A provider emails that Terrence has missed two planning meetings and asks whether his services should be reduced because he is not engaged. Marisol notices that both meetings were scheduled for early morning, when Terrence has told her his medication makes it hard to be alert. The provider's message frames the absences as a choice, but Marisol sees a possible access issue that has not been discussed with Terrence at all.
lessons.question: What should Marisol do next?
choices: Tell the provider that reducing services is reasonable because missed meetings show Terrence does not want support.
Talk with Terrence about what times and formats work for him, reschedule accordingly, and ask her supervisor or the ADA coordinator if a formal modification question comes up.
Ask Terrence's psychiatrist to confirm in writing that he has a disability before changing anything.
feedback: Missed meetings do not establish refusal or lack of interest. Terrence has described a possible scheduling barrier that needs examination before anyone draws that conclusion or proposes a service reduction.

This is the strongest response. It treats the absences as a possible access barrier, asks Terrence directly, makes a simple change that is within Marisol's role, and routes any formal ADA question to the office that decides it.

The case describes an ordinary scheduling adjustment, not a request to determine eligibility. Ask about workable times without collecting unnecessary clinical information; route any formal documentation question to the person or area responsible.
lessons.reflection: Think about a recent situation in your work where someone's participation was described as a lack of motivation. What other explanations could you have considered?
lessons.action: Review one standard process you use, such as meeting scheduling or deadline reminders, and write down one way it could be adjusted for someone whose symptoms vary by time of day or week.

check.question: Which statement best describes the Olmstead decision?
check.correct: Unjustified segregation of people with disabilities is discrimination, and public entities must offer community services when appropriate, not opposed by the person, and reasonably accommodated.
wrong: It applies only to people with intellectual disabilities and does not cover people with mental illness.
It requires states to close all institutions regardless of a person's needs or wishes.
check.feedback: The case involved two women with mental illness and intellectual disabilities. The Court tied community-based treatment to professional appropriateness, the person not opposing it and reasonable accommodation in light of state resources and others’ needs. Counsel should assess how the decision and current requirements apply.

lessons.title: Recovery, stigma and diagnostic overshadowing
objectives: Explain what a recovery orientation means in disability services planning.
Identify how stigma can shape case notes, referrals and provider decisions.
Describe diagnostic overshadowing and why it matters for people with intellectual or developmental disabilities.
Draft a neutral, behavior-based description to replace a labeling statement.
lessons.teaching:
The federal Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration describes recovery as a process of change through which people improve their health and wellness, live self-directed lives and strive to reach their full potential. Recovery need not mean that every symptom has ended. It is an individual process that can include treatment, support, meaningful activity and choices about one’s life. For disability services, a recovery orientation fits naturally with person-centered planning: start with what matters to the person, build on strengths, and support the person’s goals without predicting a single course of recovery.

Stigma works against recovery in small, repeated ways. A case note that says a person is noncompliant, manipulative or attention seeking travels from file to file and shapes how new staff and providers see them. Labels like these describe an interpretation, not a behavior. A more useful note records what happened, what the person said they needed and what was tried. Neutral language protects the person's dignity, and it also makes the record more accurate for everyone who relies on it later, including staff who check the record and the person themselves, who has a right to see much of what is written about them.

Diagnostic overshadowing is an error that stigma and assumptions can contribute to. It happens when a new sign of distress is assumed to be part of an existing disability instead of being checked as a separate health or mental health concern. For people with intellectual or developmental disabilities, a change in sleep, appetite, mood or behavior may be written off as the disability when it could signal depression, anxiety, trauma, pain or a medical problem. A 2026 umbrella review reported higher estimates for some conditions, including schizophrenia, while estimates for others were lower and could reflect underdiagnosis. The included reviews ranged from moderate to critically low quality. Methods and populations differed, and important groups were underrepresented. These findings support careful assessment; they cannot diagnose an individual or establish the cause of a change.

You are not the person who makes a diagnosis. You are often the person who notices a change first, or who reads a provider report and asks whether anyone has looked into it. When behavior changes, describe what was observed and help the concern reach the appropriate professional. Follow urgent safety and required reporting procedures without waiting for a routine review. A review does not itself authorize restrictions on the person’s activities.
lessons.keyPoint: Recovery can include continuing symptoms while a person pursues their own goals. When a change occurs, consider whether a separate health need has been overlooked and seek appropriate assessment.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Jonah reviews incident reports for 245D providers. A report about Adaeze, who has an intellectual disability, says she has become aggressive and has stopped eating with housemates, and that this is typical for her diagnosis. Jonah checks earlier reports and sees no similar incidents in the past year. The provider's plan proposes more structure and fewer outings. Nothing in the file shows that anyone has asked Adaeze what has changed or arranged a health or mental health check.
lessons.question: What should Jonah do next?
choices: Ask the provider and case manager whether a medical and mental health review has been arranged, and whether anyone has asked Adaeze what has changed, before the plan is narrowed.
Accept the provider's explanation because staff who see Adaeze daily know her best.
Flag the provider for a licensing violation because the report uses labeling language.
feedback: This is the strongest response. It asks about a possible overlooked health need and includes Adaeze’s account. Follow urgent safety and reporting duties promptly; a health review does not itself authorize restrictions.

Daily staff insight is valuable, but a sudden change is exactly the situation where assumptions about a diagnosis can hide a new health or mental health need. Accepting the explanation without a check could delay care.

The language in the report is worth addressing, but jumping to a violation finding does not answer the more urgent question about Adaeze's health. Formal licensing determinations also follow their own process and office.
lessons.reflection: Recall a phrase you have seen in case files that labels a person rather than describing what happened. How might it have shaped the next reader's view?
lessons.action: Using the fictional case or an approved training example, replace three labels with observable descriptions, the person’s account and what was tried. Do not copy private case records into a learning exercise or silently overwrite a historical note.

check.question: What is diagnostic overshadowing?
check.correct: Attributing a new symptom or change to an existing disability so that a separate health or mental health condition is overlooked.
wrong: Giving a person too many diagnoses so that the main disability is hidden.
A clinician's decision to keep a diagnosis private from the support team.
check.feedback: Diagnostic overshadowing happens when a known disability becomes the explanation for everything. It can delay treatment for depression, anxiety, pain or medical illness, especially for people with intellectual or developmental disabilities. Staff do not diagnose, but they can ask whether a change has been checked.

lessons.title: Crisis resources and crisis planning in Minnesota
objectives: Identify the main crisis options described by DHS, including 988, county and Tribal mobile crisis teams and follow-up crisis services.
Distinguish a mental health crisis response from a medical emergency that requires 911.
Plan how to help a person build a crisis plan in advance using their own preferences.
Explain how crisis calls connect to provider reporting duties under the Positive Supports Rule.
lessons.teaching:
The Minnesota Department of Human Services tells people who are thinking about suicide or having a mental health crisis to call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and to call 911 for a medical emergency. People can also contact their local mobile crisis team directly. DHS keeps a directory of mental health crisis phone numbers by county and Tribe, and describes crisis services as available around the clock across the state. Because numbers and local arrangements change, point people to the current DHS directory rather than keeping an old list in a desk drawer.

DHS describes mobile crisis teams as mental health professionals and practitioners who provide psychiatric services in a person's home or another place outside the usual clinic setting. Mobile responders can meet the person at home or another chosen location. Residential crisis services offer a short stay in a facility. Crisis stabilization follows a crisis response and helps the person connect with ongoing providers and build skills. These services have different purposes; ask the current service contact what is available and appropriate. Response arrangements depend on the situation and local resources. Do not promise a particular response time or that emergency services will never become involved. Follow current emergency guidance when there is immediate danger or a medical emergency.

Develop a crisis plan before a crisis, when the person can take part with any communication support they need. A useful crisis plan is written with the person, in their words. Discuss early warning signs, helpful responses, preferred contacts and services, and what the person wants responders to know. Include health details only where appropriate in the authorized care plan, and explain how the plan will be accessed and shared. Preferences guide planning but do not remove applicable emergency or reporting duties. A trauma-informed plan avoids forcing the person to retell painful history and focuses on what they want others to know.

For license holders covered by the Positive Supports Rule, specified crisis events also carry reporting duties. The Positive Supports Rule requires license holders to report certain events to DHS on the behavior intervention report form, including an incident that requires a call to mental health mobile crisis services and a behavioral incident that results in a call to 911. Use the full rule and current DHS instructions to identify reportable events; this is not a list of every duty. A report can prompt examination of support needs, but its presence alone does not establish a cause, poor care or a violation.
lessons.keyPoint: Use current crisis resources and plan with the person before a crisis. Covered providers must identify and report the events specified by the Positive Supports Rule; a report alone does not explain what happened.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Imani supervises case managers at a county lead agency. During a team meeting, a case manager mentions that Walt, who receives waiver services and lives in his own apartment, called her late one night in distress, and she did not know whom to call besides 911. The team realizes their printed crisis list is out of date and that few of the people they serve have written crisis plans. Walt has said before that police at his door frightens him.
lessons.question: What should Imani do next?
choices: Tell case managers to call 911 in every situation to be safe.
Leave crisis planning to mental health providers because it is outside disability case management.
Replace the printed list with a link to the current DHS crisis directory, and set a goal for case managers to help each person who wants one write a crisis plan, starting with Walt.
feedback: Emergency services are appropriate for medical emergencies or immediate danger. A blanket instruction overlooks the other crisis options DHS describes. Assess the situation through current procedures and consider Walt’s preferences without promising a particular response.

Case managers coordinate services across systems. Crisis planning is part of person-centered support, and mental health providers can contribute, but the case manager is often the one who can bring it together.
This is the strongest response. It fixes the out-of-date information, uses DHS as the authoritative source and builds a person-centered crisis plan that reflects Walt's own preferences.
lessons.reflection: If someone you serve called you in crisis tomorrow, how confident would you feel about your next step? What would make you more confident?
lessons.action: Find the current DHS mental health crisis phone directory for the counties or Tribes you work with, save the link where your team can reach it, and check that it matches any printed materials you hand out.

check.question: According to DHS, which option is designed to send trained responders to a person's home or a place the person chooses during a mental health crisis?
check.feedback: Mobile crisis response brings one or two trained responders to the person. Residential crisis services offer a short stay in a facility, and crisis stabilization follows a crisis to connect the person with ongoing supports. Knowing the difference helps you explain choices to people and families.

lessons.title: Working across mental health and disability services
objectives: Describe how CADI waiver eligibility and adult mental health services such as ARMHS can fit together in one person's plan.
Identify gaps that appear when mental health and disability systems each assume the other is responsible.
Plan a coordinated, person-centered team conversation that respects data privacy rules.
Explain how trauma-informed participation and required service procedures can work together during a service change.
lessons.teaching:
Many people with psychiatric disabilities use both disability and mental health services. The DHS Community-Based Services Manual describes the Community Access for Disability Inclusion, or CADI, waiver. A person must choose community living and meet all eligibility criteria. These include Medical Assistance eligibility, disability certification through Social Security or the State Medical Review Team, and being under sixty-five when first opening to the waiver. MnCHOICES must assess a need for nursing-facility level of care and for supports beyond the Medical Assistance state plan. A psychiatric diagnosis alone does not establish eligibility. The responsible assessors and eligibility staff must confirm each requirement using the current manual.

Adult mental health services can sit alongside waiver services. The DHS provider manual describes Adult Rehabilitative Mental Health Services, often called ARMHS, as services that help adults develop psychiatric stability, social skills, personal adjustment and independent living skills when those abilities are affected by symptoms of mental illness. People may also work with mental health targeted case managers, therapists, psychiatric prescribers and crisis teams. Each has a different role, funding source and set of rules. ARMHS and waiver services are not interchangeable, and providers must coordinate overlapping services to avoid duplicate services and billing.

The risk is a gap in the middle. When each service treats a concern as another team’s responsibility, the person may be left to connect them. Identify the unresolved task and who has authority to address it, rather than assuming that a diagnostic label assigns all responsibility to one program. A person-centered approach puts the person's goals first and asks each part of the team what it contributes. Coordination still has to respect privacy. The Minnesota Government Data Practices Act and health privacy laws limit what can be shared and with whom, so get the person's informed consent or confirm the legal basis before sharing, and ask your data practices contact when unsure.

Trauma-informed practice asks how to make the conversation safe, understandable and responsive without requiring a personal trauma account. Do not infer someone’s history from a diagnosis. Explain choices and limits, ask what would help participation and follow through on agreed responsibilities. Required safety action, reporting and lawful service procedures continue alongside this approach.
lessons.keyPoint: People with psychiatric disabilities often need both disability and mental health services. Close the gap between systems through person-centered coordination that respects data privacy and avoids repeating harm.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Rosa is a DSD program consultant helping a county resolve a stuck case. Kwame receives CADI waiver services in an apartment and also sees an ARMHS practitioner. His waiver provider says his hoarding and missed rent are a mental health issue; his ARMHS practitioner says housing problems are for the waiver team. Kwame has told his case manager he is afraid of losing his apartment and being sent back to a facility. No one has met together, and Kwame has not been asked who he wants involved.
lessons.question: What should Rosa suggest?
choices: Suggest the case manager ask Kwame whom he wants involved, confirm valid consent or another legal basis for the proposed information sharing, and agree on who does what toward his goal of keeping his home.
Recommend that the waiver provider end services because the issues are clinical.
Ask each provider to send Rosa its records so she can decide which system is responsible.
feedback: This is the strongest response. It centers Kwame’s goal and identifies responsibilities across the services. Confirm which information may be shared, with whom and for what purpose; participation in the same team does not create unrestricted access.
Ending waiver services because a problem is labeled clinical is exactly the gap this lesson describes. It raises the risk that Kwame loses his home and moves to a more restrictive setting.
Collecting records without Kwame's consent and without a clear legal basis risks a data practices violation, and it keeps the decision away from the person it affects.
lessons.reflection: Where in your own work do handoffs between systems tend to stall? What is one question that could get a stalled handoff moving?
lessons.action: Use Kwame’s fictional case to list the tasks that need coordination and the roles that could address them. Identify what permission or legal basis would be needed to share information. This exercise does not authorize access to actual case files.

check.question: Which statement about coordinating care across mental health and disability services is most accurate?
check.correct: Staff should confirm the person's informed consent or another legal basis before sharing private data, even when coordination would help.
wrong: Any provider on the team may share any information with any other provider because they all serve the same person.
Mental health information can never be shared with disability services staff under any circumstances.
check.feedback: Minnesota's Government Data Practices Act and health privacy laws allow sharing in some situations and limit it in others. The safe habit is to get informed consent or confirm the legal basis first, and to ask your data practices contact when you are not sure.

cards.back: A mental health condition can qualify as a disability when it substantially limits a major life activity, including when episodic symptoms are active. Disability protections and eligibility for a specific service are separate questions.

The Supreme Court decision holding that unjustified segregation of people with disabilities is discrimination under Title II of the ADA. Minnesota's Olmstead Plan sets state agency goals to carry it out.
SAMHSA describes recovery as a process of change through which people improve their health and wellness, live self-directed lives and strive to reach their full potential.
Assuming a new symptom or change is part of an existing disability, so a separate health or mental health condition goes unrecognized.
Trained crisis responders who come to a person's home or a place the person chooses. DHS lists county and Tribal crisis numbers, and people can also call or text 988.
Adult Rehabilitative Mental Health Services: Medical Assistance services that help adults build psychiatric stability, social skills and independent living skills affected by mental illness.

aid.heading: Spot the rights question
items: Ask whether a person's psychiatric disability is affecting access to a meeting, deadline, service or setting.
Try simple, within-role changes first, such as a different time, format or reminder.
Route formal ADA, reasonable modification or legal risk questions to the ADA coordinator or legal counsel.
Remember that the Olmstead decision still stands even when federal enforcement guidance shifts.

aid.heading: When behavior changes
items: Compare with past reports to see whether this is new.
Ask the person what has changed, in a way that does not require retelling trauma.
Seek appropriate health assessment and follow urgent safety and reporting duties. A review alone does not authorize restrictions.
Replace labels such as noncompliant with a description of what happened and what was tried.

aid.heading: Crisis readiness
items: Use the current DHS crisis directory by county and Tribe, not an old printed list.
Share 988 for call, text or chat, and 911 for medical emergencies.
Plan before a crisis with the person and any communication support they need; explain confidentiality and emergency limits.
Covered providers must report the events specified in rule 9544.0110, including incidents requiring mobile crisis calls and behavioral incidents resulting in 911 calls. Check all applicable duties.

aid.heading: Coordinating across systems
items: Start with the person's goal and ask whom they want involved.
Get informed consent or confirm the legal basis before sharing private data.
Agree in writing on who does what, and set a date to check progress.
Check current CADI and mental health service rules in the DHS manuals before advising.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Human Services — Mental health crisis response
sources.note: Supports the guidance to call or text 988, call 911 for medical emergencies, use the county and Tribal crisis directory, and the descriptions of mobile crisis, residential crisis and crisis stabilization services. Check the directory for current local numbers.

sources.title: Minnesota Olmstead Implementation Office — Minnesota's Olmstead Plan
sources.note: Describes the state plan’s purpose, identifies the next plan as a draft and affirms Minnesota’s commitment after the June 2026 federal opinion.

sources.title: U.S. Department of Justice, ADA.gov — Statement on Enforcement of the Integration Mandate of Title II of the ADA and Olmstead v. L.C.
sources.note: Historical federal technical assistance. Its account of the Court’s holding is checked against the opinion itself; do not treat every enforcement position on this page as current after the June 2026 OLC opinion.

sources.title: SAMHSA — Recovery and Recovery Support
sources.note: SAMHSA’s recovery framework emphasizes self-direction, strengths and multiple pathways. Its working definition is retained; course applications do not predict an individual’s recovery.

sources.title: BJPsych Open — Prevalence of mental disorders in people with intellectual disabilities across the lifespan: umbrella review (2026)
sources.note: The 2026 umbrella review discusses diagnostic overshadowing, possible underdiagnosis and varied prevalence estimates. Included reviews ranged from moderate to critically low quality; findings do not diagnose individuals.

sources.title: Minnesota DHS Community-Based Services Manual — Community Access for Disability Inclusion (CADI) Waiver
sources.note: Supports the CADI eligibility criteria summarized in Lesson 4. Waiver rules change; check the current manual page before advising.

sources.title: Minnesota DHS MHCP Provider Manual — Adult Rehabilitative Mental Health Services (ARMHS)
sources.note: Supports the description of ARMHS purpose and general eligibility. Clinical eligibility is determined by qualified providers, not by disability services staff.

sources.title: 42 U.S.C. 12102 — Definition of disability
sources.note: Supports the ADA definition and treatment of episodic impairments, records of disability and regarded-as coverage.

sources.title: U.S. Supreme Court — Olmstead v. L.C., 527 U.S. 581 (1999)
sources.note: Primary court decision; community-based treatment is subject to the professional, individual-choice and reasonable-accommodation conditions explained in the opinion.

sources.title: DOJ Office of Legal Counsel — June 18, 2026 opinion on institutionalization
sources.note: Identifies the dated executive-branch interpretation, distinct from the Supreme Court decision and Minnesota’s plan.

sources.title: Minnesota Rule 9544.0110 — Reporting restrictive interventions and incidents
sources.note: Identifies reportable events for covered license holders, including mobile crisis incidents and behavioral incidents resulting in 911 calls.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes 144.293 — Release or disclosure of health records
sources.note: Consent and specified legal exceptions govern release of health records; consult the responsible data practices staff about the actual disclosure.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes 13.05 — Duties of responsible authority
sources.note: Addresses limits on government data collection, use and dissemination, including informed consent and legal authority.
